description: Brittonic kingdom in the Clyde valley (c. 500–1034) speaking a P-Celtic language related to Welsh; one of the last survivals of Romano-British culture in northern Britain, its gradual absorption into the kingdom of Scotland and replacement of Brittonic by Gaelic represents the extinction of one of the oldest linguistic traditions in the British Isles.

temporal.notes: Brythonic kingdom; absorbed into Scottish realm.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Alt Clut British kingdom consolidates around Dumbarton Rock.
Rhydderch Hael and successors; Strathclyde independent Briton kingdom.
Dumbarton sacked; kingdom rebuilds around Govan.

rise_factors.description: Dumbarton Rock, Alt Clut, was one of the strongest natural fortresses in Britain; it controlled Clyde valley access.
Strathclyde maintained distinct royal lines through catastrophic Viking raids, showing institutional resilience.
Strathclyde Britons maintained mounted warfare traditions that made them effective in the northern British political arena.
Strathclyde's center at Dumbarton Rock, Alt Clut, was one of the most defensible positions in Britain, allowing the Briton kingdom to survive Viking raids, Scots pressure, and Anglian expansion.

Strathclyde preserved Brittonic culture and language in the northwest long after Anglo-Saxon conquest elsewhere, maintaining an indigenous P-Celtic identity that survived the initial collapse of Roman Britain.

decline_factors.description: Viking sack of Dumbarton Rock 870 was catastrophic; Olaf and Ivar of Dublin besieged and destroyed it.
Scottish kingdom under Kenneth mac Alpin's successors progressively absorbed Strathclyde through dynastic union.
Strathclyde kings became sub-rulers under Scottish overlordship in the 10th century.

A Norse-Irish fleet besieged and captured Dumbarton Rock in 870 after a four-month siege, sacking the fortress and carrying off thousands of captives, a catastrophic blow from which Strathclyde never fully recovered.
Strathclyde was progressively absorbed by the emerging Kingdom of Alba through the 10th–11th centuries, with the last independent kings being replaced by Scots royal princes as sub-kings.
